title: Candy Thief
description:
At 12 years old, I created my first video game during a two-week summer camp at SMU focused on designing 2D platformers. That experience sparked a passion for game development that has driven every project since.

Building Candy Thief taught me the basics of game creation: image editing in Photoshop, coding in C#, and the planning and organization it takes to actually finish a project. It laid the foundation for everything that followed.

title: Debugging
description:
Over three months, my team and I built this game for the Texas Technology Student Association's statewide video game design competition. I was assigned a team with no prior game design experience, so I steered us toward a 2D platformer since it was a genre they could actually contribute to while still giving me room to add more complex features.

I handled all the scripting and a big chunk of the level design. The competition theme that year was 'TSA Based,' and we took it literally: players could switch between careers mid-game and use job-specific abilities to solve puzzles. The Architect could build objects into existence, and the Robotic Engineer could deploy a small controllable robot to get through tight spaces.

The story follows a computer infected by a virus, and players have to solve puzzles and 'debug' the system before it's destroyed. I put over 500 hours into this project, making it the most complete and polished PC game I've ever made.

We ended up placing in the state competition finals. This was also my first time really working on a game with a team, and I learned a lot about collaboration, code documentation, and just how different it is to build something with other people. It's one of my proudest projects.

title: Fade
description:
Fade was actually my third attempt at making a mobile game, and the first one that made it to the Play Store. In 2018, I tried building a 2D platformer where the screen would be dark and light up as you explored, but I couldn't figure out how to pull it off in Unity with my skillset at the time. My second attempt that same year was an endless side-scroller where you tap to make a ball jump, but I kept running into JDK configuration issues and never got it to build for mobile.

In 2019, I came back to the idea with a fresh approach. I kept the limited-visibility concept and built a casual game around it: players drag their character to dodge rectangles that get faster over time. This time I got the JDK working and even added a Google Play leaderboard connected to players' Google accounts.

Once the game felt polished enough, I bought a Google Developer License and published it. Beyond the game itself, this project taught me a lot about the business side of game development: putting together a store listing, managing a release, and understanding what it actually takes to get a game in front of real players.

title: Future Me
description:
This is the only project on this site that started as a school assignment, and honestly it's a good example of how I tend to use Unity for things beyond just making games. My sophomore English teacher assigned a college research presentation, so I turned it into a 3D driving experience where players drive down different paths to learn about each of the three schools I researched.

I built it in about a week, and it was one of my first real attempts at 3D game design. The driving mechanics came together better than I expected, and it was a fun reminder that a game engine can be a useful creative tool for a lot more than just games.

title: Minion Mania
description:
I went back to SMU's two-week game design camp in 2015 with a specific goal in mind: make something for my 6-year-old sister, who was really into the Minions from Despicable Me. I ended up building a 2D arcade game just for her, and it turned out to be one of the more fun projects I'd done at that point.

It pushed me outside the typical platformer format and challenged me to make most of the visuals myself using Photoshop. It was also the first time I wrote scripts entirely on my own without relying on camp examples or resources, which was a big deal for me at the time.

title: Neon Signs
description:
Neon Signs is an educational game built around the idea of making handwriting practice actually enjoyable. Players take on the role of a custom neon sign business owner and work through writing challenges that get progressively harder. They get feedback on their handwriting to help build consistency, and the game keeps them motivated through rewards like unlocking new sign colors and a history screen to track progress.

The trickiest part was building the handwriting analysis system, which I had no prior experience with. I used the Google Cloud Vision OCR API to check whether the player's written words were correct, then added separate handwriting capture logic to evaluate other factors like writing time, cursive level, stroke smoothness, and standard deviation. It required a lot of research and trial and error to get right.

This project pushed me to grow as both a developer and a designer. Figuring out how to give feedback that was actually specific and useful ended up being just as challenging as the technical side of things.

title: The Adventures of Nock Fletcher
description:
After Debugging placed at the TSA competition, I wanted to step things up for the next year. The plan was to use a new render pipeline, build a full 3D world, and create something that looked noticeably better than what other teams were submitting. Then COVID-19 canceled the convention, and we never got the chance to compete. Without that deadline, the team lost motivation and the game never got finished.

Even in its incomplete state, I'm proud of what we put together. The game follows an experienced archer on his way to a castle archery tournament, using different types of special arrows to solve puzzles across various zones. Each arrow type had multiple uses: bomb arrows could clear obstacles, ice arrows could freeze enemies, chain arrows could create ziplines or climbing paths, and so on.

As the main scripter and one of the level designers, I spent most of my time getting the mechanics to feel right, which came at the cost of finishing the levels themselves. The game is unoptimized and incomplete, but this project probably taught me more than any other. I picked up skills in 3D modeling, animation, shader development, sound design, and photo editing that I hadn't really touched before.

title: COVID-19 Time Capsule
description:
When my world history class assigned a pandemic time capsule project, I built mine in Unity. The game lets players explore five apps that got really popular during COVID-19, each with a short description, all presented inside a fake phone UI I made from scratch.

About halfway through, I felt like the experience was too flat without any real gameplay. So I added a 3D environment and taught myself real-time terrain modification to build a digging mechanic. Now players have to dig up the capsule before they can explore it, which made the whole thing feel a lot more interactive.

Beyond being a class project, it was a good excuse to practice UI/UX design inside a game engine, and a good reminder that adding a little extra to something can make a big difference.

title: Time Management
description:
This was my first full game in over a year, made for the Texas Aggie Game Developers' semesterly game jam. I chose to work with a team of beginners, partly to help them learn and partly just to ease myself back into 2D game design.

I handled the programming, helped with game design decisions, and ran our weekly group meetings. We originally planned a 2D puzzle platformer, but after getting feedback from the organization we pivoted to an endless 2D tower defense game. It was a more manageable scope for everyone given how much schoolwork we had going on. Even with the simpler format, I still tried to design mechanics that made the gameplay feel interesting rather than just functional.

It was a good refresher for me, and a solid reminder of how much I enjoy working on a team and building something together.

title: Vaccination Destination
description:
This was built in 24 hours during the Texas A&M Howdy Hack, my first hackathon. The event was held entirely online because of COVID-19, and our team of four had to plan, design, and build something in a single day.

After spending so much time on more complex 3D projects, going back to a simple 2D platformer was actually a nice change of pace. We didn't get very far with the levels, but that was kind of expected given the time frame. The real value was learning how to move fast, make decisions quickly as a team, and ship something functional under a tight deadline.
